2018_118_022718regmtg.paragraph: Agenda packet for the Troy Board of Education regular meeting of February 27, 2018 at the Services Building. It sets the district's enrollment posture for 2018-2019 against Fred Ignatovich's projection of 13,207 students — closing Barnard, Bemis, Schroeder, Boulan Park and both high schools to open enrollment except for up to 25 incoming ninth graders transferring to Athens, while opening a limited Schools of Choice program for 40 kindergarten, 3 first grade and 14 middle school seats. Business awards $55,865.00 of fiber maintenance to Fiber Link, Inc. and $188,971.00 of general trades work to R&E Development, and the December 2017 Treasurer's Report carries total disbursements in period of $13,132,669.57.

**Meeting**
Regular meeting, February 27, 2018, 7:00 PM, Services Building, 4420 Livernois.

**Recognition**
Four items: the 2017-2018 Senior Scholar Athletes, who must maintain a 3.5 cumulative grade point average while participating in an athletic program; the Fall 2017 All-State Athletes; a Mission Moment on the Troy High Auto Lab with David Easterbrook; and Principal Appreciation Month, marked by a resolution recognizing February as Principal Appreciation Month in Troy.

**Consent agenda**
Six items: minutes of the December 5, 2017 closed session, the January 9, 2018 special meeting, the January 9 closed session and the January 9 workshop, minutes of the January 16, 2018 organizational and regular meeting, and the December 2017 Treasurer's Report.

**Treasurer's Report — December 2017**
Total check disbursements are $10,949,972.44 — General Fund $9,978,994.82, Special Revenue Funds $248,358.87 and Other Funds $722,618.75 — and total disbursements in period are $13,132,669.57, including $1,972,883.34 of outgoing wire transfers, $179,070.01 of P-Card purchases and $33,022.78 of ACH debits. Within the fund breakdown, the General Fund (101) alone accounts for $9,468,981.45. (The transmittal's period line reads "December, 2018" as printed, though the registers themselves are December 2017.)

**The January 16 minutes, in brief**
The organizational meeting elected Mr. Schmidt president, Mr. Gottlieb vice president and Mr. Hauff secretary, each 6-0 with Mrs. Hammond absent, ending Dr. Philippart's seven years as president. Rick L. West was appointed treasurer for January through December 2018, twelve depository institutions named, six law firms continued as counsel, and Judy Holmes designated to post meeting notices. The Board also ratified the TESPA contract extension through June 30, 2022 and approved the $853,231.22 furniture purchase for 4th and 5th grade classrooms. Mr. Schmidt explained on the record that the corrected asbestos resolution "was just an error naming the company that was awarded the bid" — the consulting firm's name had been inadvertently used in the original.

**Curriculum — who may enroll in 2018-2019**
Dr. Machesky presents enrollment projections prepared by Dr. Fred Ignatovich of Stanfred Consultants. District headcount has climbed from 11,965 in 2005/06 to **13,084 in 2017/18**, and the projection for 2018/19 is **13,207**, rising to 13,274, 13,320, 13,325 and 13,396 through 2022/23. Actual enrollment has run ahead of both the projected and budgeted figures in each of the last three years — 13,084 actual against 12,992 projected and 12,900 budgeted in 2017/18.

On that basis administration recommends closing Barnard, Bemis, Schroeder and Boulan Park on total enrollment and space constraints, and closing Athens and Troy High again — with the exception of **not more than 25 incoming ninth grade students** who live in the Troy High attendance area but wish to attend Athens, applications accepted during a two-week window at the beginning of March. Students with siblings at Athens or Troy High in grades 9 through 11 may open enroll to remain.

Mark Dziatczak, Deputy Superintendent of Teaching and Learning, presents the Schools of Choice report first given at the February 6 workshop. Of the district's elementary students, **500 are Schools of Choice against 5,096 non-SOC — 8.93%**, ranging from 19.05% at Hill and 15.70% at Costello down to 0.95% at Schroeder. A survey of current SOC families found 40 kindergarten, 3 first grade and 14 middle school siblings planning to attend. Kris Griffor and Mark Dziatczak's February 6 memo recommends exactly those numbers, noting that on the prior year's application volume the district anticipates far more than 50 kindergarten applicants and could admit more in the third week of August if space allows.

Four separate resolutions follow, splitting each grade band between Section 105 (districts within Oakland County) and Section 105c (districts outside Oakland County whose ISD is contiguous with Oakland ISD): 40 kindergarten and 3 first grade under each of 105 and 105c, and 14 total 6th-8th grade students at Baker, Larson and Smith under each — the counts being the same students viewed from either statute, not additive.

**Business**

| Item | Award | Fund |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Fiber maintenance (Bid #9851) | Fiber Link, Inc. — $55,865.00 | General Fund |
| General trades, BP 21A | R&E Development — $188,971.00 | 2016 Capital Projects Fund |

Three fiber proposals came in — Amcomm at $75,791.00, Fiber Link at $45,865.00 and Turnkey Network Solutions at $29,651.62. John Foster of Convergent Technology Partners recommends Fiber Link despite Turnkey's lower base bid, because Turnkey underestimated the work and its higher hourly rates would exhaust a time-and-materials contract faster. The award adds Voluntary Alternates for CAD prints of the outside and building fiber routes ($7,500.00 and $2,500.00) to reach $55,865.00. The service is newly eligible for E-rate Category 1 reimbursement of roughly 40%.

The general trades package covers roller shades, window sills, platform and ceiling work at Costello, Leonard, Martell and Morse, plus remodel work at Troy Union and hollow metal doors at Troy High, Athens and IA East. Barton Malow disqualified low bidder Titan Retail Industries for omitting a required allowance and, after a post-bid interview, recommended R&E Development at $188,971.00.

**Other**
The Board adopts its 2018 committee assignments, approves Vice President Steve Gottlieb's attendance at the NSBA Annual Conference in San Antonio, April 7-9, 2018, and casts its ballot in the MASB Region 8 election among Donald Hubler (incumbent, Macomb ISD), Robert McLachlan, Birgit McQuiston and Darlene Pomponio, Ph.D.

Agenda packet for the regular meeting of the Troy School District Board of Education, February 27, 2018, 7:00 PM at the Services Building, 4420 Livernois, Troy, MI 48098. The agenda is: 1. Pledge of Allegiance; 2. Recognition — A. Senior Scholar Athletes 2017-2018, B. All-State Athletes Fall & Winter 2017-2018, C. Mission Moment: THS Auto Lab – David Easterbrook, D. Principal Appreciation Month; 3. Additions & Deletions; 4. Public Communication (agenda items); 5. General – Consent Agenda; 6. Personnel; 7. Curriculum — A. Report: Enrollment Projections, B. Consideration: Schools Closed to Open Enrollment, C. Report: Schools of Choice 105 & 105C, D. Consideration: Schools of Choice 105 – Elementary, E. Consideration: Schools of Choice 105C – Elementary, F. Consideration: Schools of Choice 105 – Grades 6-8, G. Consideration: Schools of Choice 105C – Grades 6-8; 8. Business — A. Consideration: WAN Fiber Maintenance, B. Consideration: General Trades – Costello, Leonard, Martell, and Morse Elementary Schools; 9. Public Communication (non-agenda items); 10. Other — A. 2018 Board Committee Assignments, B. NSBA Annual Conference & Exposition, C. 2018 MASB Board of Directors' Election; 11. Adjournment. Meetings are cablecast on TS-TV Channel 19 (Comcast) and Channel 15 (WOW) every Monday and Wednesday at 2:00 and 9:00 p.m. when school is in session, and viewable at http://vimeo.com/troyschools.

**Recognition 2.A: Senior Scholar Athletes 2017-2018.** The Board welcomes and acknowledges senior scholar athletes from winter and spring sports; to achieve the distinction a student must maintain a 3.5 cumulative grade point average while participating in an athletic program. The packet prints the full roster of roughly 115 seniors by name, sport and school across Athens and Troy High — cross country, football, boys and girls soccer, boys tennis, girls golf, girls swim and dive, volleyball and fall cheerleading.

**Recognition 2.B: All-State Athletes, Fall 2017.** Ten students are named all-state in their sports, read out by Mr. Jolly: Gabriel Brown (freshman, Athens, tennis), Brennan Cimpeanu (sophomore, Troy High, tennis), Darius Feier (senior, Troy High, boys soccer), Steven Forman (senior, Troy High, tennis), Spencer Liu (senior, Troy High, tennis), Joseph Mason (senior, Troy High, boys soccer), Jessica Robinson (sophomore, Troy High, volleyball), Michael Song (junior, Troy High, tennis), Cole Valentine (senior, Athens, boys soccer) and Megan Worrel (senior, Troy High, cross country).

**Recognition 2.C and 2.D.** The Mission Moment features the Troy High School Auto Lab with David Easterbrook; the January 16 minutes elsewhere in this packet record that the Auto Lab had been highlighted on Channel 7 news and would have a booth at the International Auto Show at Cobo Hall. Principal Appreciation Month follows: throughout Michigan, February has traditionally been celebrated as Principal Appreciation Month in recognition of the work of building-level educational leaders, and the resolution recites that energetic and inspiring school leadership is essential if teachers, schools and districts are to ensure all Troy students are college and career ready, that K-12 principals act as the liaison between the school and the community it serves, and that Troy principals are dedicated, quality educational professionals — resolving that the Troy Board of Education officially recognizes February as Principal Appreciation Month in Troy.

**Consent agenda.** A. Minutes of the December 5, 2017 Closed Session Meeting; B. Minutes of the January 9, 2018 Special Board of Education Meeting; C. Minutes of the January 9, 2018 Closed Session Meeting; D. Minutes of the January 9, 2018 Board of Education Workshop; E. Minutes of the January 16, 2018 Board of Education Organizational and Regular Meeting; F. Treasurer's Report – December 2017.

The December 5 and January 9 closed sessions were both held to discuss support-staff contract extensions — the Troy Education Secretarial Association (TESA) on December 5, the Troy Educational Support Personnel Association (TESPA) on January 9 — with no other business conducted. The January 9 special meeting adopted resolution 18-001 going into closed session on the TESPA extension under Section 8(c) of the Michigan Open Meetings Act, Public Act 267, on a roll call with Mr. Miletti absent. The January 9 workshop covered public communication, an ALICE Crisis Response overview presented with Steve Brandimore from Safe-Ed and School Resource Officer John Julian of the Troy Police Department, and the 4th and 5th grade classroom furniture purchase.

**The January 16, 2018 organizational and regular meeting minutes.** President Philippart called the meeting to order at 7:00 p.m.; in addition to Dr. Philippart, Board members Fleming, Gottlieb, Hauff, Miletti and Schmidt were present and Mrs. Hammond was absent. All four high school student representatives attended, along with Superintendent Machesky, administrators Birmingham, Dziatczak, Griffor and Harris, and approximately 35 members of the audience. Every vote that evening carried 6-0 with Hammond absent.

Dr. Philippart served as acting chairperson (18-002) and appointed Judy Holmes temporary secretary. Mrs. Fleming nominated Mr. Schmidt for president (18-003), who was elected until December 31, 2018 on a 6-0 roll call. Mr. Miletti nominated Mr. Gottlieb for vice president (18-004), elected 6-0. Mr. Gottlieb nominated Mr. Hauff for secretary (18-005), elected 6-0. Resolution 18-006 appointed Rick L. West, Assistant Superintendent, Business Services, as Treasurer of the Troy Board of Education for January through December 2018.

Resolution 18-007 adopted the Fund Depositories and Investments resolution, naming Bank of America, Bank of New York, Charter One Bank, JP Morgan Chase Bank, Comerica Bank, First Merit Bank, Fifth Third Bank, Flagstar Bancorp, MILAF (the Michigan Liquid Asset Fund Plus, managed by PFM Asset Management, Inc. through Fifth Third Bank), Morgan Stanley Smith Barney, PFM Securities, Inc. through Fifth Third Bank, and PNC Bank. Monies may be withdrawn by checks bearing the facsimile signature of Treasurer Rick West, and in emergencies the handwritten signature of the Treasurer or of Superintendent Richard M. Machesky on the General Fund and Payroll accounts at Bank of America; Troy Career Center accounts at PNC Bank are drawn on the handwritten signature of the Career Center Manager, Assistant Manager or Program Coordinators; the Comerica account for health care and dependent care flexible spending claims may be drawn by ACH debit to Next Generation Enrollment, Inc.; funds are invested according to Board Policy 5000.06; and the Treasurer is authorized to combine money from more than one fund for an investment authorized by subsection (1)(h) of Section 380.1223 of the Revised School Code, with the maximum amount to be invested regulated by the school code. Gary N. Hauff certified the resolution as Secretary.

Resolution 18-008 continued the designation of Clark Hill, PLC; Collins & Blaha, P.C.; Lusk Albertson; LaPointe & Associates, P.C.; Thrun Law Firm, P.C.; and Beier Howlett, P.C. as legal counsel for the 2018 calendar year, with the superintendent authorized to consult additional counsel as needed on prior notification to the board. Resolution 18-009 continued the designation of the Superintendent as Deputy Secretary; 18-010 designated Judy Holmes, Secretary to the Superintendent of Schools, as the person for posting notices of meetings for 2018; and 18-011 adopted the schedule of meetings for the 2018 calendar year.

The consent agenda that night (18-012) approved the December 5, 2017 special meeting and workshop minutes, the December 19, 2017 meeting minutes, the Treasurer's Report for November 2017 and the corrected resolution from the 12/19/17 asbestos abatement. Mr. Schmidt mentioned that the corrected resolution for asbestos abatement was just an error naming the company that was awarded the bid — the name of the consulting firm had been inadvertently put in the initial resolution — and that the December 19 meeting minutes would also reflect the correction. Resolution 18-013 approved the extension of the TESPA, MEA/NEA contract through June 30, 2022. Resolution 18-014 approved the personnel recommendation, recorded in these minutes as new hires Rebecca Turner and Jill Flaherty. Resolution 18-015 approved the furniture purchase for 4th and 5th grade classrooms in the amount of $853,231.22 through Workspace Interiors by Office Depot and the Oakland County America Saves Cooperative Purchase Program as an expenditure of the 2016 Capital Projects Fund; Dr. Philippart asked whether the district could donate the old desks as it had with the last furniture purchase, and Mr. Dziatczak said the district was looking into that.

Student representatives reported: Anjana Pisupati (IA-East) on enrollment applications, a HOSA competition at which over 70 medals were won, and the IASA Cultural Show; Nadia Shaouni (Troy College & Career High School) that 32 students began winter semester college classes at Oakland, Macomb and Washtenaw Community Colleges through Dual Enrollment; Tori Zarbaugh (Athens) on the ScreenAgers screening and Charity Week; and Hana Barre (Troy High) that Judge Hartig held court in school and that Activist Week funds would benefit elementary schools in Flint. Board members thanked Dr. Philippart for seven years as president — Mr. Miletti, Mr. Hauff, Mr. Gottlieb, Mrs. Fleming and Mr. Schmidt each spoke — and Dr. Machesky presented her a wood gavel and plaque; each Board member received a framed print of the district's four characteristics of World Class. The meeting adjourned at 8:01 p.m.

**Treasurer's Report, December 2017.** Rick West transmits the check register including current period voids, together with listings of ACH debits, wire transfers and P-Card purchases, certifying that the disbursements were payments made for obligations of the Troy School District and that all materials or services listed on the invoices have been received or performed. By fund: General Fund (101) $9,468,981.45; Grant Fund (120) $2,834.75; Special Education Fund (122) $507,178.62; Durant Funds (140) nil; Food Service Fund (520) $32,834.06; Troy Career Center (529) $72,518.62; Community Education Fund (530) $143,006.19; Facilities Rental Fund (535) nil; Debt Funds (312, 314, 315, 316) nil; Building & Site Funds (499, 414, 416) $493,040.20; Student Activity Fund (700, 701) $229,578.55; Memorial Scholarship Fund (750) nil.

The totals are: Total General Fund $9,978,994.82, Total Special Revenue Funds $248,358.87, Total Other Funds $722,618.75, TOTAL CHECK DISBURSEMENTS $10,949,972.44 — a figure the check register itself confirms at TOTAL REPORT 10,949,972.44 — plus ACH debits $33,022.78, outgoing wire transfers $1,972,883.34 and P-Card purchases $179,070.01, less prior period void disbursements of $2,279.00, for TOTAL DISBURSEMENTS IN PERIOD $13,132,669.57. The transmittal's period line is printed as "December, 2018" beside the meeting date of February 27, 2018, evidently a typographical error for December 2017, which is what the underlying wire transfer, ACH and P-Card reports are labeled. The December wire transfers are dominated by payroll: $782,938.97 and $784,565.55 of payroll taxes for the 12/15/17 and 12/01/17 runs, $150,644.01 and $154,699.14 of payroll TSA, and $33,612.93 and $34,632.98 of payroll HSA. The middle sections of the packet are the December check register run by fund, roughly 2,300 register lines.

**Curriculum 7.A: enrollment projections.** Dr. Machesky presents to the Board on enrollment projections for the 2018-2019 school year and beyond, with analysis of the district's enrollment history and projections provided by Frederick R. Ignatovich, Ph.D. of STANFRED Consultants.

The enrollment history runs from 11,965 in 2005/06 upward through 12,068 (2006/07), 12,126 (2007/08), 12,165 (2008/09), 12,069 (2009/10), 12,056 (2010/11), 12,328 (2011/12), 12,391 (2012/13), 12,573 (2013/14), 12,556 (2014/15), 12,710 (2015/16), 12,868 (2016/17) to 13,084 in 2017/18 — a gain of more than eleven hundred students over twelve years, and a period in which the district grew rather than shrank.

Projected versus actual enrollment is tabulated by year (projected / budgeted / actual): 2013/14 12,494 / 12,440 / 12,573; 2014/15 12,653 / 12,590 / 12,556; 2015/16 12,612 / 12,560 / 12,710; 2016/17 12,710 / 12,740 / 12,868; 2017/18 12,992 / 12,900 / 13,084; and 2018/19 projected 13,207 and budgeted 13,207 with actual not yet known. In each of the last three years the actual exceeded both the projection and the budgeted figure. The methodology slide explains that future enrollments would be expected to fall between the MOST LIKELY and LOW projections, calculated by adding MOST LIKELY plus the LOW divided by two.

The birth-to-kindergarten ratio table runs 4.65 (05-06), 4.94 (06-07), 5.45 (07-08), 5.29 (08-09), 5.22 (09-10), 5.63 (10-11), 5.67 (11-12), 5.94 (12-13), 6.18 (13-14), 5.82 (14-15), 6.39 (15-16), 6.59 (16-17), 6.53 (17-18) and a projected 6.50 for 18-19. Projected future total K-12 enrollment is 13,207 for 2018/19, 13,274 for 2019/20, 13,320 for 2020/21, 13,325 for 2021/22 and 13,396 for 2022/23.

**Curriculum 7.B: schools closed to open enrollment for 2018-2019.** Administration has reviewed enrollment for the elementary, middle and high school attendance areas. Because of the elementary and middle school buildings' total student enrollment and physical space constraints, it recommends that Barnard, Bemis, Schroeder and Boulan Park Schools be closed to open enrollment. The district's goal for Athens and Troy High has been to maximize each building's enrollment, which has resulted in both being closed to open enrollment for the past several years; based on current projections for 2018-2019 it is recommended that both be closed again, with the exception of not more than twenty-five incoming ninth grade students who reside in the Troy High School attendance area but wish to attend Athens High School, applications for those twenty-five spots accepted during a two-week window at the beginning of March. The resolution adopts that closure and provides that students with siblings attending Athens and Troy High currently enrolled in grades 9 through 11 will be allowed to open enroll to remain for the 2018-2019 school year.

**Curriculum 7.C: the Schools of Choice report.** Mark Dziatczak, Deputy Superintendent of Teaching and Learning, summarizes the report shared with the Board at the February 6 Board Workshop.

The elementary enrollment projections from Fred Ignatovich give, for kindergarten and first grade by year, HIGH / AVERAGE / LOW bands: 2015/2016 kindergarten HIGH 791, AVERAGE 763, LOW 733 and first grade HIGH 842, AVERAGE 748, LOW 802; 2016/2017 kindergarten HIGH 839, AVERAGE 811, LOW 784 and first grade HIGH 896, AVERAGE 798, LOW 876; 2017/2018 kindergarten HIGH 863, AVERAGE 823, LOW 782 and first grade HIGH 941, AVERAGE 822, LOW 919; and 2018/2019 kindergarten HIGH 901, AVERAGE 874, LOW 847 and first grade HIGH 927, AVERAGE 874, LOW 909.

The elementary SOC application history records openings advertised against applications received and students enrolled for kindergarten and first grade each year from 2006-2007 (25 and 25 openings, 72 and 42 applications) through 2017-2018 (55 and 5 openings, 150 and 41 applications), totalling 915 kindergarten and 310 first grade openings advertised, 1,592 and 516 applications received, and 941 and 265 students enrolled over the twelve years. Applications have consistently exceeded openings at kindergarten by a wide margin.

The data summary for 2017-2018 gives, by building, SOC students against non-SOC students with the SOC percentage and its year-over-year change: Barnard 73 / 431, 14.48% (-2.42); Bemis 16 / 538, 2.89% (-1.51); Costello 57 / 306, 15.70% (+1.00); Hamilton 62 / 458, 11.92% (-0.28); Hill 64 / 272, 19.05% (-1.75); Leonard 42 / 377, 10.02% (-0.18); Martell 52 / 435, 10.68% (-2.82); Morse 19 / 471, 3.88% (-0.62); Schroeder 5 / 522, 0.95% (-0.55); Troy Union 27 / 447, 5.70% (+0.60); Wass 62 / 360, 14.69% (-2.11); Wattles 21 / 479, 4.20% (-0.20); TOTAL 500 SOC and 5,096 non-SOC, 8.93%, down 0.97 points. By grade: kindergarten 54 SOC / 812 non-SOC, 6.24% (-4.86); first 98 / 845, 10.39% (-2.41); second 104 / 819, 11.27% (+1.47); third 79 / 796, 9.03% (-0.37); fourth 83 / 883, 8.59% (+0.09); fifth 82 / 941, 8.02% (-0.18).

By subgroup, SOC students are 21.80% ELL (109 students) against 30.85% (1,572) among non-SOC; 16.60% free/reduced lunch (83) against 12.85% (655); and 6.20% special education (31) against 9.38% (478). By ethnicity the SOC population is 58.40% White (292), 24.00% Asian (120), 8.60% Black (43), 6.60% multi-ethnic (33), 1.60% Hispanic (8), 0.60% Hawaiian/Pacific Islander (3) and 0.20% American Indian (1), against a non-SOC population that is 50.10% White (2,553), 40.09% Asian (2,043), 3.55% Black (181), 3.47% multi-ethnic (177), 2.35% Hispanic (120), 0.31% Hawaiian/Pacific Islander (16) and 0.12% American Indian (6). Non-SOC enrollment by grade for 2017-2018 runs 812, 845, 819, 796, 883, 941, 912, 949, 909, 994, 993, 922 and 994 for kindergarten through twelfth, totalling 11,769, an increase of 328.

A survey emailed to current Schools of Choice families asked about siblings eligible for kindergarten, first grade and grades 6 through 8 in 2018-2019: 40 kindergarten students plan to attend, 3 first grade students, and 14 middle school students — 7 in sixth grade, 2 in seventh and 5 in eighth.

The February 6, 2018 memorandum from Kris Griffor and Mark Dziatczak to Dr. Machesky lists the factors considered: current enrollment across the district; enrollment projections, patterns and trends; numbers and percentages of SOC students currently in the district; the projected number of SOC siblings age-eligible to enter in 2018-2019 under a limited program; and available elementary classrooms. They recommend using Fred Ignatovich's 1.5 enrollment projection numbers with his recommended formula (most likely plus low, divided by two) as the foundation, and accepting SOC applications for 40 kindergarten, 3 first grade and 14 middle school students — noting that on the prior year's application volume the district anticipates attracting many more than 50 kindergarten applicants, which would allow it to admit 40 initially with the option of admitting more in the third week of August if space allows, and that middle school students would be placed in a building according to available space.

**Curriculum 7.D through 7.G: the four Schools of Choice resolutions.** Michigan law requires a district to pass a resolution each school year if it intends to participate in a Schools of Choice program, and Troy adopts four — the same seat counts stated once under Section 105 and again under Section 105c, distinguishing where the applicant's home district sits rather than adding seats.

7.D adopts, under Section 105 of the State School Aid Act of 1979 as amended by Public Act 300 of 1996, acceptance of applications for a Limited Schools of Choice program for 2018-2019 for 40 nonresident kindergarten and 3 nonresident first grade students who attend a school district within Oakland County (total students include non-Oakland County residents – Section 105c). 7.E adopts the same 40 kindergarten and 3 first grade seats under Section 105c for students attending a school district outside Oakland County, if that intermediate school district is contiguous with the Oakland Intermediate School District boundaries (total students include Oakland County residents – Section 105).

7.F anticipates that seats will be available for 2018-2019 in grades 6 through 8 at Baker, Larson and Smith Middle Schools and adopts, under Section 105, acceptance of applications for 14 total nonresident 6th-8th grade students at those buildings with placement based on building availability, for students attending a district within Oakland County. 7.G adopts the identical 14 total seats under Section 105c for students attending a district outside Oakland County whose ISD is contiguous with Oakland ISD.

**Business 8.A: fiber maintenance.** An RFP was issued to obtain competitive bids for the district's fiber cabling maintenance, reviewed by Beth Soggs, Director of Technology, and John Foster of Convergent Technology Partners. Foster's January 29, 2018 recommendation letter on Bid #9851 records that bids and proposals were received, opened and publicly read at 2:30 p.m. on January 8, 2018. Three proposals came in: Amcomm at $75,791.00, Fiber Link, Inc. at $45,865.00 and Turnkey Network Solutions at $29,651.62, with several voluntary alternates offered by Fiber Link. All proposals were compliant, but variations in the interpretation of bid items required clarification from several vendors to compare unit items and hourly rates accurately.

At first glance Turnkey appears lowest, but Foster found that Turnkey underestimated the amount of work involved, that its hourly rates are higher, that on a time and material contract those higher rates would use up the allocated amounts faster than Fiber Link's, and that Fiber Link's lower hourly rates will let the district accomplish more and maximize the refunds available under E-rate. He recommends award to Fiber Link, Inc. together with Voluntary Alternates 1 and 2 as proposed, which provide accurate documentation of the fiber routing inside and outside the buildings: base bid $45,865.00, Voluntary Alternate #1 $7,500.00 for CAD prints of the outside fiber cable routes and Voluntary Alternate #3 $2,500.00 for CAD prints of the building fiber cable routes, for a total award of $55,865.00. (The letter's prose refers to alternates 1 and 2 while the pricing table labels them #1 and #3.) Fiber Link is the incumbent contractor for the district's fiber maintenance and has already amassed significant knowledge of the network. The letter stresses that this is primarily a time and material contract, provided on an as-needed basis, put out to bid now because the service has become eligible for reimbursement under E-rate Category 1, under which the district will receive a reimbursement of approximately 40% of its expenditures up to 40% of the approved amount.

The attached Universal Service Funding service provider evaluation worksheet scores each bidder across six weighted factors — cost (30 points maximum), integration and service transition (25), adherence to specifications (15), prior experience with the district (15), financial stability and capability (10) and prior experience providing similar services (5). Fiber Link scores 88.8 of 100 against 65.0 each for Amcomm and Turnkey; Turnkey takes the full 30 points on cost but scores zero on prior experience with the district. No bidders were disqualified. The resolution awards fiber maintenance to Fiber Link, Inc. in the amount of $55,865.00 as an expenditure of the General Fund.

**Business 8.B: general trades at Costello, Leonard, Martell and Morse.** An RFP was issued for competitive bids on architectural components — roller shades, window sills, platform and ceiling work — at Costello, Leonard, Martell and Morse Elementary Schools; the bid also included remodel work at Troy Union Elementary and doors at Troy High, Athens and International Academy East. Bid responses were reviewed by Rob Carson, Director of Operations, and Barton Malow.

Christa Amalio, Barton Malow project manager, writes to Rick West on February 6, 2018 regarding the 2013 Bond Program, Series 2, Bid Package 21A. The first bidder, Titan Retail Industries, was missing an allowance noted in the work scopes, which was reason to disqualify it from award. The second apparent low bidder, R&E Development, submitted a breakdown not in alignment with the other bids received even though its overall amount was second among the bidders. At the post-bid interview the estimator explained that all the work at all of the buildings was included in the base bid total price, and that having received his hollow metal door pricing late he placed the total door cost on the Martell Elementary price line rather than breaking the door pricing out by building. Asked about the new wall at Athens and the low price at Leonard, he admitted he had not spent much time on the bid form and was rushing to deliver the bid on time. Through the interview the contractor proved knowledgeable of the drawings and had received quotes from vendors similar to the other bidders and compliant with the specifications, and was able to provide the necessary information and qualifications to receive a recommendation for award. The recommendation is category 06000 General Trades to R&E Development at $188,971.00, total awards $188,971.00. The resolution awards bid pack 21A to R & E Development in the amount of $188,971.00 as an expenditure of the 2016 Capital Projects Fund.

**Other 10.A: 2018 Board committee assignments.** Each year Board members are selected to serve as representatives to committees of state and national board associations, within the community, within the school district and within the Board's own committees. The attached membership list assigns: Oakland Schools' Legislative Committee and Oakland Schools' Designate to Gottlieb and Hauff; Friends of Troy Seniors Advisory Committee, Troy Community Coalition and Troy Foundation for Educational Excellence to Fleming; Troy Parks and Recreation Board and Troy Youth Assistance to Hauff, Philippart and Schmidt across the community slate; Troy Nature Society to Hammond; Troy Historical Society to Hauff; the Continuous Improvement Team 17-18 and Diversity Council to Hammond; the Crisis Committee and District Technology Committee to Miletti; the Wellness Committee to Fleming and Hammond; the Policy Committee to Gottlieb, Hauff and Philippart; and the Superintendent Evaluation Committee to Gottlieb, Schmidt and Miletti.

**Other 10.B: NSBA Annual Conference & Exposition.** Board Policy 1000.01, Organization and Functioning of the Board; Reimbursement of Expenses, provides that any expenditure of district funds for members for out-of-state meetings must have prior approval by resolution. Board Vice President Steve Gottlieb has indicated his desire to attend the National School Boards Association Annual Conference & Exposition in San Antonio, Texas, April 7-9, 2018, and the resolution approves his attendance as representative of the Troy Board of Education. The packet reproduces the NSBA registration materials, which note that NSBA events are open to U.S. school districts holding membership in their state school boards association and that NSBA reserves the right to cancel the registration of any board member or employee of a district not in good standing, in which event NSBA is not liable for hotel, airfare or other charges.

**Other 10.C: 2018 MASB Board of Directors' election.** Biographical data for the candidates is attached. Region 8 is a three-year term with one seat and four candidates: Donald Hubler of Macomb ISD, Macomb County, the incumbent; Robert McLachlan of Romulus Community Schools, Wayne County; Birgit McQuiston of Lake Orion Community Schools, Oakland County; and Darlene Pomponio, Ph.D. of Southgate Community Schools, Wayne County. The resolution casts the Troy Board of Education's ballot for one candidate.

Cheryl Huffman's January 25, 2018 email from MASB explains the mechanics: seven seats are up for election, one candidate is unopposed and one Region and Group has no candidates, so ballots will be distributed only for Regions 1, 5, 7 and 8. Each district receives one ballot, emailed to the superintendent secretary on record with MASB. Electronic voting is a two-step process — submit the ballot, then confirm it has been submitted. The ballot deadline is 1 p.m. on Wednesday, March 7, 2018; unofficial results will be available on a voicemail recording after 2 p.m. on the deadline date, and official results approved at the March 16, 2018 Board of Directors' meeting. No local district or ISD funds may be used to campaign for anyone running for a seat.

Read as a whole, the February 2018 packet is the district's annual enrollment-policy meeting. A projection of 13,207 students for 2018-2019 — the thirteenth consecutive year of growth off a 2005/06 low of 11,965 — drives the decision to close six buildings to open enrollment while admitting 40 kindergartners, 3 first graders and 14 middle school students under Schools of Choice, essentially the number of siblings already identified in the district's own survey. The two capital awards, $55,865.00 of fiber maintenance and $188,971.00 of general trades work, are modest by comparison and both flow from the 2013 bond program's second series and the district's E-rate posture.
